title: IIT Madras Orders Students to Delete Instagram Videos Supporting Jantar Mantar Protests
excerpt: The premier institute directed students to remove social media posts backing the CJP-led agitation, as campuses across India face pressure to silence protest voices.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • IIT Madras ordered students to delete videos supporting the Jantar Mantar protests.
  • The directive followed a viral video showing solidarity with hunger-striking students.
  • IIT Roorkee also advised against political discussions on social media.
  • Protests against the Modi government are escalating, with significant student participation.
  • Activist Sonam Wangchuk's hunger strike has intensified public outrage.
IITs Crack Down on Student Expression
›IIT Madras instructed students to remove protest-related posts.
›IIT Roorkee urged avoidance of political discussions.
›Both directives align with government efforts to suppress dissent.
›Students express concern over free speech limitations.

IIT Madras has directed its students to take down Instagram videos expressing solidarity with the ongoing Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, according to students who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The instruction was relayed through the institute's Dean, who asked faculty advisors to convey the order to student groups. A message shared by one student read: "Guys, we were asked by the Dean to take down the posts related to the Jantar Mantar protests. Our faculty advisor was called. We will be taking down those posts, including the solidarity video. Since you guys had contributed to the video, we thought it was important to let you know."

The directive followed a short video that went viral on social media showing IIT Madras students holding a banner reading, "Solidarity with Jantar Mantar protest. Solidarity with Wangchuk and students on hunger strike. Students' lives matter."

IITs Tighten Grip on Campus Expression

IIT Madras is not alone. IIT Roorkee also issued an advisory urging students and employees to stay away from political discussion on social media and to avoid statements that could "embarrass" the institute's relationship with the central government, according to MediaNama.

Indian authorities have also been blocking and restricting online content documenting police violence and internet shutdowns during the student protests, with at least one Instagram reel by Maktoob Hindi geo-blocked in India after Meta received a legal request under the IT Rules.

A Movement That Outgrew Its Origins

The CJP began as a satirical Instagram account created by Boston University graduate Abhijeet Dipke in May, after India's chief justice made comments widely interpreted as calling unemployed youth "cockroaches." What started as dark humor quickly crystallized into a political force.

The movement sharpened its focus around allegations of NEET entrance exam paper leaks that forced millions of students to re-sit the test. Its primary demands include the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan and government accountability for the suicides of NEET aspirants.

"People are assuming this is only a NEET issue, education... I must tell you this is just the beginning. We will also come to election issues."

— Abhijeet Dipke, CJP founder

Climate activist Sonam Wangchuk joined the protest on June 28 with an indefinite hunger strike. By his 25th day, he had lost approximately 11 kilograms. On July 19, Delhi police removed him from the protest stage, bundled him into a sheet, and took him to Medanta Hospital in Gurugram — a moment captured on video that intensified public anger.

Protests Escalate Across the Country

On July 20, thousands of students marched toward Parliament in a "Chalo Sansad" rally on the opening day of the Monsoon Session. Police responded with tear gas and baton charges, drawing comparisons to some of the largest anti-government demonstrations in years. Delhi Metro shut 16 stations, and shops in Connaught Place announced closures.

From a hospital bed on July 22, Wangchuk offered to break his fast if the government assured no force would be used against protesting students and no FIRs or punitive action would be filed against participants.

"I request the government not to use force again on students and do not file any charges or FIRs. I need an assurance for that. If I get that assurance, I will break my fast today."

— Sonam Wangchuk, activist

Health Minister JP Nadda agreed to meet CJP spokesperson Saurav Das on Monday, a sign the government is beginning to engage. The opposition Congress party, led by Rahul Gandhi, organized a sit-in near the Prime Minister's residence at Lok Kalyan Marg.

A Sensitive Moment for India's Premier Institutes

The IIT Madras directive puts India's elite technical institutes at the center of a free-speech debate. These institutions, which produce graduates who fill engineering and technology roles worldwide, have historically maintained a careful distance from political agitation. The move to suppress student voices aligns them visibly with the government's effort to contain the protests — a posture that risks drawing scrutiny from alumni networks and international academic circles.

Mumbai witnessed its own large student protest on Wednesday, and CJP has urged the government not to take action against participants in the July 20 march.

Growing Student Protests Across India
June 28
Sonam Wangchuk joins protests with an indefinite hunger strike.
July 19
Wangchuk is forcibly removed from protest stage by police.
July 20
Thousands of students march toward Parliament; police respond with force.
July 22
Wangchuk offers to end hunger strike if government assures no force against students.
image_caption: IIT Madras campus in Chennai. The institute directed its students to remove Instagram videos expressing solidarity with the Jantar Mantar protests led by the Cockroach Janta Party.
nri_angle: IIT alumni form a significant segment of the Indian diaspora, and the crackdown on campus free expression has drawn concern from overseas graduates and Indian student organizations abroad.
author: Diaspora Desk
